entities.summary: Pope Gregory I, commonly known as Saint Gregory the Great, was the 64th Bishop of Rome from 3 September 590 until his death on 12 March 604. A member of the Roman aristocracy, Gregory was born around 540 AD in Rome, Italy, to a wealthy family. He was educated at the Gregorian Ecolage and later studied law in Rome before becoming a priest. Gregory's early career was marked by controversy, including a dispute with the Roman Prefect, Anthimus I, over the appointment of a new bishop. However, he eventually won the support of the Roman people and was elected bishop in 590. Gregory's papacy was marked by significant reforms, including the creation of a new system of government for the Church and the establishment of the office of the Papal Nuncio. He also played a key role in the conversion of the Anglo-Saxons to Christianity, leading a mission to England in 597 and consecrating Augustine of Canterbury as the first Archbishop of Canterbury. Gregory's legacy extends beyond his own time, influencing the development of the Catholic Church and shaping the course of European history. He was canonized as a saint by the Catholic Church in 859 and remains one of the most revered figures in Christian history. The city of Gregory, Italy, is named in his honor, and the Gregorian Chant, a style of sacred music, is also a testament to his enduring legacy.
